_purpose: Research log. Key = the specific thing looked up; value = what was found, verdict, and the exact URLs so it is never researched twice.
_rules: One entry per distinct question. Update the entry when re-checking a version. Never delete a URL that a decision rests on.

schema.question: what was being decided
findings: facts, with version/tag attached
schema.verdict: what we do because of it

entries.question: What Python and libraries exist in the build sandbox, and can pip install?
findings: Python 3.11.2, pip 23.0.1, 2 vCPU, 3.6 GiB RAM, no swap, ~20 GB disk.
Nothing preinstalled: no numpy, zstandard, torch, lightning, transformers, pytest, maturin.
pip download from PyPI works (numpy 2.4.6 wheel fetched at ~100 MB/s).
zstandard 0.25.0 has manylinux/mac/windows cp311 wheels; torch 2.15.0 wheels: 514 MiB linux x86_64, 461 MiB aarch64, 132 MiB macOS arm64, 121 MiB win_amd64.
torch wheels exist for cp311-cp314 plus free-threaded cp314t.
entries.verdict: Pure-Python archx is buildable and testable here; torch integration tests are local-possible but heavy (514 MiB download) so full matrices go to CI.

entries.question: Which hosts can this sandbox reach?
findings: Reachable: github.com, api.github.com, codeload.github.com, pypi.org, files.pythonhosted.org, registry.npmjs.org.

Blocked (curl 000, no connection): static.rust-lang.org, sh.rustup.rs, crates.io, index.crates.io, static.crates.io, docs.rs, doc.rust-lang.org, raw.githubusercontent.com, objects.githubusercontent.com, release-assets.githubusercontent.com, docs.github.com, example.com.
github.com release-asset URLs answer 302 but the redirect target is blocked.
entries.verdict: No Rust toolchain can be installed here, ever. GitHub file content must be read through the API (contents endpoint), not raw. Docs must be written from API-read sources.

entries.question: What can the GitHub token do in this repo?
findings: actions/workflows: 200 (currently 0 workflows). actions/runs: 200. actions/artifacts: 200.
actions/secrets: 403. actions/variables: 403. actions/permissions: 403. branches/main/protection: 403.
contents: 200 read. X-Oauth-Scopes header empty; fine-grained token style permissions.
entries.verdict: We can create commits and read workflow metadata, but never logs, artifacts, secrets or variables. Therefore every workflow must commit its results into the repo, which is exactly the user's stated workaround.

entries.question: Which public optimizer hook does archx attach to, and since which version?
findings: v2.0.0 has register_step_pre_hook / register_step_post_hook (lines ~298/320).
v1.13.1 has only the internal profile_hook_step decorator, no public hook.
post hooks run after func(*args, **kwargs) inside profile_hook_step, i.e. after the weights are updated.
profile_hook_step patches the optimizer CLASS lazily on first step (_patch_step_function), so the first step pays a one-time patch cost.
entries.verdict: attach() uses optimizer.register_step_post_hook; minimum torch is 2.0 for attach(), 2.1 for the accumulate-grad hook. Deltas therefore come from a shadow copy of the previous step (Architecture section 4).

entries.question: Since which torch version can we observe gradients cheaply without a backward hook?
findings: Tensor.register_post_accumulate_grad_hook exists at v2.1.0 and v2.9.0, absent at v2.0.0.
It is defined on torch._tensor.Tensor (line ~572 at v2.4.0), not on nn.Module.
The hook fires right after the gradient for that tensor has accumulated, before zero_grad.
entries.verdict: Preferred gradient-norm path on torch >= 2.1: one hook per tracked parameter, no full backward hook. Fallback: read param.grad in the optimizer pre-step hook.

entries.question: What does the HF Trainer callback expose, and when can archx read gradients and the trainer object?
findings: Callback methods take (args, state, control, **kwargs); the Trainer is reachable via kwargs when provided.
Available: on_train_begin/end, on_epoch_begin/end, on_step_begin/end, on_pre_optimizer_step, on_optimizer_step, on_substep_end, on_log, on_evaluate, on_save, on_predict.
on_pre_optimizer_step and on_optimizer_step are absent in 4.44 and present in 4.46.
Inner loop order in current trainer.py: optimizer.step() -> model.zero_grad() -> global_step += 1 -> on_step_end, so gradients are zero by on_step_end.
entries.verdict: Default gradient capture is an optimizer post-hook on trainer.optimizer (version independent). on_pre_optimizer_step is used when >= 4.46. Minimum supported transformers for Tier 2 is 4.46, with a silent fallback below it.

entries.question: What is wrapped by Accelerate/DDP and how does that affect parameter access?
findings: Trainer creates an Accelerator; model may become DistributedDataParallel (extra 'module.' name prefix) and the optimizer becomes AcceleratedOptimizer (its step() is what runs, and it can skip steps).
In the DDP case every rank holds identical full parameters; in FSDP/ZeRO cases it does not.
entries.verdict: Names come from accelerator.unwrap_model(model); the observed optimizer is the wrapped one; only the main process writes to the file. Sharded setups are detected and degraded (Architecture 5.4).

entries.question: Do TRL SFTTrainer/DPOTrainer and Axolotl's trainer accept a plain TrainerCallback?
findings: class SFTTrainer(_BaseTrainer) and class DPOTrainer(_BaseTrainer) in current TRL.
class AxolotlTrainer(...) in axolotl core/trainers/base.py subclasses the same Trainer hierarchy.
DPO-style trainers run more than one backward per optimizer step (policy and reference).
entries.verdict: No separate adapters: one ArchxCallback covers all three. Step accounting must key on optimizer steps, not backward passes.

entries.question: Which Lightning callbacks exist, and where are gradients available?
findings: Hooks include on_fit_start/end, on_train_batch_start/end, on_before_backward, on_after_backward, on_before_optimizer_step, on_before_zero_grad, on_validation_*, on_save_checkpoint, on_exception.
Automatic optimization runs the optimizer with a closure (Closure/_optimizer_step), and may call zero_grad inside the closure; manual optimization does not.
Lightning can call optimizer.step() itself or via the closure, so one step per batch cannot be assumed.
entries.verdict: Use on_before_optimizer_step (post-clipping gradients) as the default capture point, plus an optimizer post-hook for deltas; count steps from loop state. on_after_backward is available for pre-clipping norms.

entries.question: Which zstd binding should a pure-Python archx use?
findings: zstandard 0.25.0 windows/mac/linux wheels for cp311 and friends, ~5 MiB.
CPython 3.14 ships a stdlib compression.zstd package (Lib/compression/zstd present on the 3.14 branch).
lz4 exists but trades ratio for speed; not needed for a background writer.
entries.verdict: Use zstandard, with a stdlib compression.zstd path on Python >= 3.14 and a pure-fallback 'no compression' mode when neither is importable.

entries.question: Can a Rust core (Rust + PyO3/maturin) be built in this environment?
findings: No rustc/cargo/rustup installed; apt has no rustc candidate.
Every Rust distribution and crate host is unreachable from the sandbox.
Only GitHub, PyPI and npm are reachable.
entries.verdict: A Rust core can never be compiled or unit-tested locally. The v1 core is Python; a native accelerator is an optional later add-on built only on CI. Recorded as a decision for the user in Open_Questions Q4.

entries.question: Does the trigger-file workflow work, can all three runners commit results back, and what hardware do they give us?
findings: Push touching Actions/triggers/tests.txt started workflow 'tests' automatically (run 43052619656).
3 of 3 matrix jobs succeeded: ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest.
Each runner committed its own file (three separate bot commits, no conflicts) - the rebase-retry script works.
Measured cpu_count=4 on Linux x86_64, Windows X64; macOS-26.7.2 arm64. Python 3.11.18 / 3.11.9.
gathered local pulls worked as the only way to read results (Actions logs remain unreadable).
entries.verdict: The CI spine is proven and is the transport for everything heavy. 4 vCPU per runner is 2x the sandbox, which confirms the 'heavy work goes to Actions' rule.

entries.question: Which package names are free for this project on PyPI and npm?
findings: PyPI archx: 200, version 0.1.1, 'A framework to explore the design space of computer systems' - unrelated project.
PyPI archx-mdl, archxmdl, archx_mdl, archnemix, archx-lifeline: 404 (free).
npm archx: 404 (free). npm archx-mdl: 404 (free).
npm username existence cannot be checked unauthenticated (401 for both archx and archnemix).
PEP 503 normalises archx.mdl and archx-mdl to the same project name, so both pip spellings resolve.
entries.verdict: Distribution archx.mdl on PyPI, npm archx as a signpost, import/CLI stay archx. Re-check right before publishing; availability can change.

entries.question: What did implementing the container teach that the spec did not say?
findings: struct.Struct with '<' uses standard sizes and no alignment: '<HBBQIIII' is exactly 28 bytes, not 32.
argparse's --version action raises SystemExit(0) instead of returning, so callers/tests must expect it.
A footer shares the byte space a block prefix would occupy, so readers must test the END magic before any size-based branch.
The step must live in the block prefix (8 bytes) for recovery to rebuild an index without decompressing payloads.
pytest -q prints only dots when everything passes; the counts have to be derived from the dot line, not from a summary sentence.
entries.verdict: Block prefix is 28 bytes with the step inside; reader checks END magic first; test records parse dots into counts.

entries.question: Which delta encoder is smallest, and at what error, on realistic training deltas?
findings: 256x256 f32, 1% moved: sparse 3,404 B exact (77x); int8 2,098 B at 8.9e-3 (125x); lowrank refused.
256x256 f32, all moved: int8 56,190 B at 1.1e-2 (4.7x); sparse refused; lowrank refused; dense_raw 242,475 B exact (1.1x).
rank-4 structure: lowrank found rank 4 exactly, 7,680 B (34.1x, 8.4e-8); int8 52,266 B at 1.5e-2; dense_raw 243,459 B exact (1.1x).
Sparse vs int8 crossover: int8 is smaller at every density from 0.1% to 100% when error is allowed; sparse only wins when exactness is required.
Byte-plane shuffle: sparse 1% 4,533 -> 7,774 B (0.58x, a loss); dense 242,473 -> 227,533 (1.07x); rank-4 243,457 -> 233,010 (1.04x). An all-zero tensor is shuffle-invariant.
Low-rank refuses random noise at rank 8 with a 1e-3 budget (relative error stays ~0.9).
Re-run 2026-11-12 after the Phase 3 source changes: identical encoder choices, and the dense_raw figures moved by <3% (zstd stream layout), which is the noise floor of these scripts.

Claim 5 re-run on the same date, 262,144 params, 200 steps: none 3.63 ms; adaptive default 3.75 ms (+3.4%, 18,443 KiB, 23 stored / 177 skipped); every step 4.53 ms (+24.7%, 57,671 KiB). The run varies by a percent between invocations, so read these as a range, not a precise figure.
entries.verdict: Policy is per tensor: exact path = sparse or dense_raw, lossy path = int8 unless the delta is genuinely low rank. Shuffle stays off by default. Any ratio quoted in the docs must come from these scripts.

entries.question: What does attaching the recorder actually cost per optimizer step, and which half costs it?
sources: local timings, 2 vCPU sandbox, torch 2.15.0+cu132 on CPU
findings: Charged cost of the recorder's own code: 0.119 ms per step with data_level=none, 0.140 ms with segments, on a 19.2 ms step (512-wide MLP, batch 1024, median of 25).
Wall-clock overhead of timing two whole runs is unusable here: the same loop varies by +/-8% between runs, and the first measurement of the same code gave +550%, +320% and -0.6% on consecutive runs.
Taking the snapshot twice per anchor cost +17% before it was removed; hashing and compressing the batch on the training thread cost +81% before it was moved to the writer thread.
content_id (blake2b-16) of 128 KiB = 210 us, of 2 MiB = 3.4 ms; zstd level 3 of 128 KiB = ~530 us; detach().cpu().numpy().tobytes() of a 2 MiB tensor = 150 us.
Global grad norm via pow(2).sum().item() per tensor = 40 us; via one numpy dot per tensor = 19 us, on a 6-tensor model.
On a 0.3 ms toy step the same code is a 350-650% overhead because framework dispatch dominates; a fixed percentage budget is only meaningful on a step big enough to have a cost.
entries.verdict: Measure by charging our own code, not by differencing two noisy runs. Data hashing and compression belong on the writer thread; the one unavoidable training-thread cost is one buffer copy, and data_level is the escape hatch. The <5% claim is stated for the weight half, where it is 0.6%.

entries.question: If the training process is killed while recording, what survives, and what must the recorder do to keep the join?
sources: Tests/integration/test_crash_recovery.py (child process, real SIGKILL on POSIX, terminate on Windows)
findings: A killed process never writes a footer, so the file is 'crashed' by definition; Reader(allow_torn=True) already read a valid prefix before any recovery, and recover_in_place then makes it closed and re-indexed without inventing blocks.
Data written only at close was lost entirely on a kill: the deltas survived and every batch did not. The product's answer became 'the weights moved' with no cause.
Writing data after each stored step introduced two ordering rules: a shard before the segment pointing at it, and movement before the data explaining it.
A segment may still not name a step the file has not reached; the flush that writes a segment is clamped to the previous step, because the EVENT for the current step is appended after the flush.
A writer-thread exception used to kill the thread silently while training continued: a dict-mutation race at step 22 lost 4000 further steps with no signal.
A segment stated several times (as it grows) is resolved by last-statement-wins in Timeline.segments(); the raw block list is append-only and not the reader's view.
entries.verdict: Write data during the run, in a fixed order, under a lock; state a segment only for steps already on disk; never let the writer thread die without recording the fault in an INFO block and re-raising it from close().

entries.question: How can torch be installed so the adapter is tested for real instead of skipped?
sources: https://pypi.org/pypi/torch/json (2.15.0, CUDA build as the default wheel)
findings: pip install torch installs 2.15.0+cu132; import fails with ValueError: libcublasLt.so.*[0-9] not found.
pip install --no-deps torch installs but stays unimportable.
The CPU index https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu is unreachable from this sandbox: TLS handshake closed (SSLZeroReturnError), no version list returned.

Installing nvidia-cublas, -cuda-runtime, -cuda-nvrtc, -cudnn-cu13, -cufft, -cusolver, -cusparse, -curand, -nvjitlink, -nccl-cu13, -nvtx, -cuda-cupti, -cusparselt-cu13, -cufile and -nvshmem-cu13 makes import work; nvshmem is the one pip does not pull in itself (libnvshmem_host.so.3).
pip then reports version conflicts against torch's pins (nccl, cusparselt, setuptools); the CPU path still imports and runs every step, so the warnings are cosmetic here.
Cost: 8 GB of disk out of 20 GB free, about 2.5 minutes of download.
entries.verdict: Install the nvidia dependency set to test the adapter locally; keep pytest.importorskip('torch') in the test module so a runner without torch skips with a reason instead of failing. Documented in Docs/Workaround.md.

entries.question: Where do loss, gradient norm, learning rate and user annotations belong in the container?
findings: The spec already allocated EVENT (5) for 'timeline entry: step, kind, values (loss, lr, grad norms, timings)' and ANNOT (7) for 'user annotation: step, event name, detail'.
The first implementation wrote both into EVENT, so a reader could not separate what the run measured from what the user declared.
META claimed capability_tier 1 unconditionally while no tier-1 value was ever written.
A tier is only meaningful compared with its own data: tier 2 without tier 1 is a claim the file contradicts.
entries.verdict: EVENT carries observations only, ANNOT carries annotations only, and the achieved tier plus every missing field with a reason goes into an INFO capability block written at close, after the data that proves tier 2.

entries.question: Does storing at a phase- and event-adaptive schedule keep a more useful history than storing at a fixed interval, for the same number of bytes?
findings: Measured on a 2000-step simulated run with 12 irregular weight jumps (steps 137, 271, 449, 613, 700, 811, 1024, 1157, 1390, 1502, 1733, 1891), both policies bisected to the same byte budget: adaptive 4,374,355 B vs fixed interval 26 4,312,597 B - 1.4% apart, so the comparison is fair.
The adaptive policy stored all 12 events (a step within 0-2 of each jump). The fixed-26 interval stored 1 of 12.

Median reconstruction error over the five steps after each event: 2.88e-03 adaptive vs 3.63e-01 fixed, a factor of 126. The file that missed the event reports weights that were true up to two intervals earlier.

On a single-jump run at a matched budget the fixed interval is actually more accurate overall (median 5.27e-03 vs 1.46e-02): a fixed grid is a fine estimator of a stationary run, and the adaptive policy spends many bytes on the dense warmup and cooldown phases.
The adaptive policy has a floor: 1% warmup plus 1% cooldown are stored densely by construction, so its spend cannot be reduced below roughly that fraction of the run.

An honest benchmark needs the jump to be visible in the loss and gradient. A pure weight jump is invisible to a policy that only sees loss, gradients and measured movement, so both policies missed it and the test measured their heartbeats instead.

The fixed baseline must have its triggers switched off. With defaults it stored 57 of its steps in the first third of a 1000-step run - it was an event-driven recorder wearing a fixed interval's name.
entries.verdict: The claim holds for its actual purpose - events - and not as a general accuracy win. The adaptive policy finds events the fixed interval cannot, at 126x lower error immediately after them; on a stationary run a fixed interval of the same size is slightly more accurate. Both results are reported; the product claim is about event resolution, and it is stated that way.

entries.question: Does the torch adapter and recorder work on architectures other than a small MLP without model-specific code?
findings: Six stacks - transformer encoder, CNN, LSTM, an elementwise gated state-space block, a 4-expert mixture with a router, and a two-tower model with a tied matrix and a frozen embedding - all go through archx.attach unchanged.

All six reach capability tier 2 (loss, gradient norms, data) and report activations as the one missing field, with a reason. No architecture is treated specially and no adapter code branches on model type.
300 steps each, seeded: 132-144 of 300 steps stored, worst per-skipped-step reconstruction error 5.6e-04 to 3.2e-03, and the loss fell on all six.
A tied matrix (text_out and shared are one storage unit) and a frozen embedding (requires_grad=False) both record and reconstruct correctly without special handling.

The sweep exposed a real trigger bug: per-region movement was the sum of each tensor's relative movement, so a transformer region of 14 tensors reported 0.20 against a 0.02 threshold when each tensor had moved 1.7%. Every step of every real run was therefore stored.
The per-region number is now ||delta||/||weights|| over the whole region, computed from accumulated squared norms, so it does not grow with the tensor count.
entries.verdict: One recorder covers every architecture tested. Region movement is a ratio over the region, not a sum over its tensors; the threshold is now comparable between models with 4 tensors and models with 400.

entries.question: Claim 7: if the optimizer post-hook is the only integration point, what is lost, and what does one line of help buy?
findings: Inside the step post-hook the gradients are still alive: the caller's zero_grad() comes after. So gradient norms need no help at all - 100% of stored steps carry one with the bare hook.
The loss and the batch are locals that die with the iteration. A bare hook records neither: tier 0, with loss, data_segments and activations all reported missing.
One recorder.log(loss=..., data=x) call before optimizer.step() moves the file to tier 2 (loss 100%, gradient 100%, data 100%) with no other change to the loop.
The hook cannot see the learning rate either, unless log() passes it; the optimizer's param group is reachable from the hook but was not read.

Help is not only about tiers: hook only stored 21 of 200 steps, hook plus log stored 44. Without a loss the policy cannot fire its loss trigger, so it falls back to phases and the heartbeat and records half as much.

Charged cost on the training thread, 200 steps on a 3-layer MLP: 0.415 ms/step hook only, 0.700 ms/step with log(). The delta is the loss conversion and the batch copy, which is what the caller asked for.

Denying a field and later offering it left both a reason and the field in the file; offering now clears the denial. Fields the run actually recorded are no longer reported missing because another field in their tier was absent.
entries.verdict: Attach in one line is honest: tier 0 with real gradient norms and real weight deltas. Tier 2 costs exactly one logging call, and the file states the difference itself rather than leaving the user to discover it. The README and the file both name what is missing and why.

entries.question: Claim 4: is a recording smaller than naive checkpointing for the same accuracy?
findings: At matched accuracy on every step of a short run, checkpointing wins: 4-9x on the six test stacks at a 1e-2 target. A stored step of ours is roughly one whole checkpoint plus overhead, so a coarse interval beats it. This is arithmetic, not a tuning problem.

At matched accuracy on the stored steps of a 1000-step run, recording wins: 0.17x-0.60x of a checkpoint at every step, i.e. 1.7x-5.9x smaller (CNN 3.8x, RNN 5.9x, multimodal 5.5x, MoE 2.9x, SSM 1.7x).
Only the recorder can be dense at an event and sparse elsewhere within one run; a checkpoint interval is uniform by construction.

The recorder is lossless at the default budget: median reconstruction error 0.0 at max_rel_error=0 and at 1e-3 (1.6e-07 worst on the MoE), and 1.4e-05-6.0e-05 at 1e-2 where int16 quantization becomes available.

Two bugs were found by building this benchmark: an off-by-one in the benchmark's own truth indexing (the file's step k is written after the k-th update), and an 'assert' written as `x = cond, "message"`, which is a tuple assignment and checks nothing.

int16 quantization shares encoding id 2 with int8 and was decoded as int8 by the reader, so every int16 delta came back half-length and failed on reshape: a file this build wrote, it could not read. The width is in the block's value dtype and the decoder is now chosen from it.

Offering int16 at the default 1e-3 budget made the default path lossy (int16 error 3.4e-5 fits inside 1e-3), which broke the documented exactness promise. int16 is offered only above the default budget.
entries.verdict: Claim 4 holds only in the form that matters for a real run: the same accuracy on the same steps, over thousands of steps. Against a checkpoint at every step the recording is 1.7-5.9x smaller; against a coarse interval tuned to the same accuracy it is 4-9x larger, and both numbers are published. The product's claim is resolution, not size.

entries.question: Does the sparse encoder still win once layers are a realistic size (4096x4096)?
sources: measured locally with archx/encoders on numpy float32 deltas, zstd compression
findings: At 4096x4096 (64 MiB of float32) with 1% of entries moved, exact sparse costs 842,049 B but int8 quantization costs 508,556 B at 1.1e-2 relative error. int8 is *smaller* than exact sparse, because zstd already collapses the quantized zeros that sparse encodes explicitly.
Same ordering at 3% and 10% density: int8 is 1.7-2.1x smaller than sparse at every density tested.

Compact raw float32 is also far smaller than the input: 1.25 MB for 64 MiB at 1% density, so "raw" is really "zstd on the raw delta" and the sparse encoder's advantage over it is only 1.5x at 1% and 1.35x at 10%.
At equal error the two are close: sparse (exact) 842 KB against int16 quantization (4.2e-5) 790 KB.

Caveat: the synthetic delta puts moved entries at random positions. A real sparse delta with structured positions (whole rows or columns) may compress differently, and this measurement cannot speak to that.
entries.verdict: The sparse encoder is worth choosing when the budget is very tight (exact or at most a few times 1e-5) and int16 is not available; it is not a size win on its own. The chooser already measures rather than assumes, so no threshold needs to be invented - but the docs no longer claim sparse is the best option for MoE or frozen-ish layers at realistic sizes.

entries.question: Claim 3: how far apart may anchors be before accumulated delta error stops being acceptable?
findings: At the default budget (1e-3) every delta is stored exactly (raw float32), so the *encoder* contributes nothing to chained error: measured 0.0 at every chain length from 1 to 64. Real reconstruction is still not bit-exact for chained steps, because a reader adds summed deltas in float32: measured 4.19e-09 absolute on weights of order 1 (relative ~1e-8), and exact at anchor steps. The two effects are separate and both are now measured.
At a lossy budget of 1e-2, the error after N quantized deltas grows sub-linearly: 7.99e-07 at N=1, 2.63e-04 at N=4, 6.62e-04 at N=16, 1.34e-03 at N=64 - i.e. 0.03x to 0.13x of the per-delta budget.
At 5e-2: 2.06e-04 at N=1 rising to 1.50e-03 at N=64, 0.03x of budget.
Even 64 deltas in one chain stay far inside the per-delta budget, so anchor spacing is not bounded by quantization accumulation at these settings.
The practical bound is not accuracy but the cost of the anchor itself: a full snapshot is what makes a long gap expensive to start from, and a crash loses the options for steps after the last anchor.
entries.verdict: Anchors are needed for recovery and deterministic reproduction, not to bound quantization error: chained quantization stays under a fifth of the per-delta budget for chains of 64, and float32 summation adds ~1e-8 relative at any spacing. Recommended spacing is stated in the spec as a recovery property (how many steps a crash may cost) and the reconstruction guarantee is 'exact at anchors, float32 rounding between them'.

entries.question: What can a Hugging Face TrainerCallback actually see, and where must a recorder attach?
sources: transformers 5.22.2: transformers/trainer.py _inner_training_loop lines ~1909-1955 (read from the installed package)
transformers 5.22.2: TrainerCallback signature list (on_pre_optimizer_step, on_optimizer_step, on_substep_end, on_log)
accelerate 1.15.0: accelerate/optimizer.py AcceleratedOptimizer.step (read from the installed package)
measured: Tests/integration/test_hf_adapter.py against a real Trainer on torch 2.15.0
findings: The loop order on a real update step is: _clip_grad_norm -> on_pre_optimizer_step -> optimizer.step() -> on_optimizer_step -> lr_scheduler.step() -> model.zero_grad() -> global_step += 1 -> on_step_end. So weights are new and gradients are alive at on_optimizer_step, and both are gone at on_step_end.
on_substep_end fires only on gradient-accumulation micro-batches (the else branch of do_sync_step), so it cannot stand in for a per-update hook - and it fires only when accumulation is configured.
state.global_step is NOT yet incremented when the step hooks fire, so it is exactly the 0-based index of the update that just happened. It is incremented before on_step_end.

Registering optimizer.register_step_post_hook on the optimizer a callback is handed raises AttributeError: that object is accelerate's AcceleratedOptimizer, which is not a torch.optim.Optimizer; the method is inherited from the Optimizer base class and reaches for _optimizer_step_post_hooks, which the wrapper lacks. It is in fact the *inner* optimizer (trainer.optimizer.optimizer) that is a real optimizer. This crashed on_train_begin, so the adapter registers no optimizer hooks and uses the callback events instead.

args.learning_rate is the initial rate; the scheduler only writes into the optimizer. The rate the update used is optimizer.param_groups[0]['lr'] read at on_pre_optimizer_step, because the scheduler is stepped after the optimizer.

Gradient norms available to any callback are the CLIPPED ones whenever max_grad_norm > 0 (default 1.0), because clipping happens before on_pre_optimizer_step. The unclipped norm is not reachable from a callback; the public per-parameter register_post_accumulate_grad_hook can reach it but never fires for a parameter whose gradient is never produced, so it would silently miss frozen or unused tensors.

on_log fires after the step record has been written and reports the MEAN loss over the whole logging window, so using it would attach a window average to the wrong step; with logging_steps=50 it would also leave 49 steps in 50 with no loss while the file still claimed tier 1. Measured: it produced losses on steps 1-3 but none on step 0, and a throttled run silently claimed tier 1 before this was fixed.

Trainer.compute_loss_func pops labels out of the inputs before the model runs, so a wrapper using that seam must rebuild the loss itself - which means guessing the loss function. Measured on a small regression model: it produced a confidently wrong number. Wrapping the instance's compute_loss instead observes the real value and leaves the run bit-identical.
A Trainer subclass that overrides compute_loss (TRL/Axolotl shape) still works, because loss_hook wraps the bound method after construction and calls it unchanged.
entries.verdict: ArchxCallback attaches at on_train_begin (model via accelerate.unwrap_model, no optimizer hook), reads gradients and the learning rate at on_pre_optimizer_step, and takes the step at on_optimizer_step keyed on state.global_step. The loss is not guessed and on_log is not used: loss_hook(trainer) or callback.log(loss=...) is the honest route, and without either the file reports tier 0 naming the way out. grad_norm_clipped is written into the metadata so a reader is never left to assume which norm it holds.

entries.question: Can a training script be recorded without editing it, and what does that injection actually capture?
sources: CPython 3.11 site.py: sitecustomize is imported during interpreter start-up, PYTHONPATH is searched before site-packages
torch 2.15.0: 'step' in torch.optim.AdamW.__dict__ is False; AdamW.step resolves to Adam.step
findings: A sitecustomize placed on PYTHONPATH does run before the target script. Verified by printing on import.

torch is NOT importable at sitecustomize time in this environment (it is a site-package, and site-packages is appended after PYTHONPATH). A prototype that did `import torch` inside try/except silently patched nothing and the training script ran to completion unrecorded.
Installing the patch from a sys.meta_path finder that wraps exec_module for 'torch.optim' works: all 15 optimizer classes with their own step were wrapped.

Patching only torch.optim.Optimizer.step counts ZERO calls for AdamW: AdamW defines no step of its own and resolves to Adam.step. Measured three AdamW steps, 0 counted. Every class that defines its own step must be wrapped.

A sitecustomize with a SyntaxError does not stop the interpreter: CPython prints 'Error in sitecustomize; set PYTHONVERBOSE for traceback' to stderr and runs the script anyway. A non-comment marker line caused exactly this. The generated file must be compiled before it is written.

An optimizer gives access to param_groups only: no model, no names, no loss, no batch, no gradients before the step. A launcher recording is therefore tier 0 with tensors named param[group][position].
atexit fires in the child, so the recording is closed and the capability block written on a normal exit.
entries.verdict: Ship the launcher as `archx run -- <command>`, as a fallback for code that cannot be edited. It installs the patch via a meta_path finder, wraps every optimizer class that defines step, compiles the injected file before writing it, and then VERIFIES the result: zero recorded steps means the file is deleted and the process exits 2 with instructions. It never claims more than tier 0.
